transforms.text: Houses were built from standardised baked and dried mud bricks, sometimes with two or more storeys.
sources: Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation (Wikipedia)
Harappan architecture (Wikipedia)

transforms.text: Houses were constructed using standardised size mud, dried mud, or baked clay bricks.
sources: Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation (Wikipedia)
Harappan architecture (Wikipedia)

transforms.text: Many buildings were constructed with two or more stories using the standardised brick units.
sources: Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation (Wikipedia)

transforms.text: Builders installed brick-lined drains, soak pits and toilets, linking house drains to covered public street drains with inspection holes.
sources: Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation (Wikipedia)
Annual Report of the Archaeological Survey of India 1926-27 (Mohenjo-daro sections)
Annual Report of the Archaeological Survey of India 1925-26 (Mohenjo-daro sections)

transforms.text: Toilet waste holes were flushed with water drawn from the house well through a clay brick pipe into a shared drain.
sources: Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation (Wikipedia)

transforms.text: House drains fed into adjacent soak pits that were periodically emptied of solid matter, possibly for use as fertilizer.
sources: Sanitation of the Indus Valley Civilisation (Wikipedia)

transforms.text: Vaulted drains and chutes were built into houses to carry off water from privies and baths to street drains.
sources: Annual Report of the Archaeological Survey of India 1926-27 (Mohenjo-daro sections)

transforms.text: Large water tanks were made watertight by laying finely fitted bricks on edge with gypsum plaster, then sealing with bitumen coating.
sources: Great Bath (Wikipedia)
Annual Report of the Archaeological Survey of India 1925-26 (Mohenjo-daro sections)

transforms.text: Tank floors and walls were paved with finely fitted bricks laid on edge set in gypsum mortar for a watertight surface.
sources: Great Bath (Wikipedia)

transforms.text: A thick bitumen layer was applied along the tank sides, and likely the floor, as an extra waterproof seal.
sources: Great Bath (Wikipedia)
Annual Report of the Archaeological Survey of India 1925-26 (Mohenjo-daro sections)

transforms.text: A sloping floor drained to a small outlet feeding a corbelled arch drain to remove used water from the tank.
sources: Great Bath (Wikipedia)

transforms.text: Streets, house blocks and courtyards were laid out in an organised plan with solid plinth foundations for adjacent structures.
sources: Annual Report of the Archaeological Survey of India 1925-26 (Mohenjo-daro sections)
Annual Report of the Archaeological Survey of India 1926-27 (Mohenjo-daro sections)
Indus Valley Civilisation (Wikipedia)

transforms.text: Solid plinth foundations were built for a group of buildings arranged together in the Sd area.
sources: Annual Report of the Archaeological Survey of India 1925-26 (Mohenjo-daro sections)

transforms.text: Streets were built solid alongside adjacent structures with underground drains running beneath them.
sources: Annual Report of the Archaeological Survey of India 1925-26 (Mohenjo-daro sections)

transforms.text: Houses were built of baked brick as part of the organised urban layout.
sources: Indus Valley Civilisation (Wikipedia)

transforms.text: Labor was mobilised collectively without a ruling elite to build shared public infrastructure, large buildings and urban planning works.
sources: Of Revenue Without Rulers: Public Goods in the Egalitarian Cities of the Indus Civilization (2022), p. 1
Killing the Priest-King: Addressing Egalitarianism in the Indus Civilization (2020)
Inequality declined in the Bronze Age city of Mohenjo-daro (2026), p. 1

transforms.text: Communities coordinated labor to build water infrastructure without relying on a distinct managerial or ruling class.
sources: Of Revenue Without Rulers: Public Goods in the Egalitarian Cities of the Indus Civilization (2022), p. 1

transforms.text: Builders avoided constructing individual-aggrandizing monuments, tombs, temples or palaces, focusing resources on shared civic structures instead.
sources: Killing the Priest-King: Addressing Egalitarianism in the Indus Civilization (2020)

transforms.text: The city's street plan and governance developed together over time, coinciding with reduced inequality between residences.
sources: Inequality declined in the Bronze Age city of Mohenjo-daro (2026), p. 1
